title: Active Exploring like a Pigeon: Reinforcing Spatial Reasoning via Agentic Vision-Language Models
one_liner: The paper gives a vision-language agent a running map of objects and a checkable list of spatial claims so it can explore, test its own guesses, and learn from dense step-by-step feedback.
lead: A vision-language agent often fails on spatial tasks because a single image does not tell it how objects relate after the camera moves. The usual setup asks the agent to answer from snapshots, so it forgets what it saw earlier and cannot check whether an intermediate guess about left, right, front, or rotation is even consistent. This paper makes the agent act, keep a scene map, and score intermediate spatial claims, because dense local feedback teaches the agent which moves improve the map and which moves break it.

problem.h2: Spatial reasoning fails when the agent cannot preserve scene structure
paras: A spatial question such as 'is the mug behind the bowl after I turn right?' needs more than object names. The agent must keep track of where each object sits, how the camera moved, and which spatial relation should stay true after the move. If it only reads one frame at a time, it loses that structure.

Sparse task rewards make this worse. If the only signal comes at the final answer, the agent does not learn which exploration step improved the map and which step made the map worse. It sees success or failure too late, so learning is slow and unstable.

callout.html: The agent needs a persistent scene map and step-level checks, because final-answer rewards alone do not teach careful spatial reasoning.

steps.text: Detect objects and their rough positions and directions from the current view.

steps.b: Write the update into a running map
steps.text: Merge the new observation with earlier ones so the agent keeps one persistent scene description.
Turn relations such as left of, behind, facing, or rotated into small executable checks.
Reward moves that make the running map support more correct claims, because those moves improve spatial consistency.
Use those dense scores to train which viewpoints and action choices help answer the final question, because moves that raise check scores usually add the evidence needed for the final decision.

paras: The paper changes the agent's internal state from a short-lived caption stream into a persistent scene map plus a bank of executable spatial checks. That change matters because the agent can now compare candidate moves by how much they improve the map, not only by whether the final answer happens to be right.
object.object: persistent scene map with executable spatial checks

hidden.name: map consistency
paras: Map consistency is the degree to which the running scene map agrees with all views collected so far and with the checked spatial claims. If the map says the chair is behind the table but a later view and the claim checker disagree, consistency drops.

This quantity is useful because it turns a vague spatial skill into a trainable signal. The agent does better when it explores views that reduce contradictions, because a more consistent map makes the final answer easier to read off.

cells: camera move adds no new evidence
heat.caption: Darker means the running map is more internally consistent and better supported by multiple views.

reads.html: The map is good when all the views and checked relations tell the same story.
The agent uses a dynamic cognitive map and Spatial Assertion Codes so that intermediate scene relations can be scored and reinforced during learning.

paras: Spatial reasoning fails from a single frozen view because many relations are hidden by viewpoint. A move that reveals the side of an object or clears an occlusion is useful only if the agent remembers what it saw before. The persistent map fixes that, because each new observation updates one shared scene state instead of replacing the old one.

The spatial checks matter because they convert 'better understanding' into something the learner can score. If a move makes more claims verifiable, the agent gets reward by improving the evidence for left-right, front-back, and orientation relations. That is more informative than waiting for the final answer, because the learner sees which local choices created a cleaner map.

The two parts help each other because the map gives the checker a place to test claims across time, and the checks tell the learner which map updates are useful. Because of that loop, exploration becomes targeted: the agent seeks views that reduce contradiction and uncertainty instead of wandering through the scene.

stages.s: Current image, past observations, and spatial question
Update object positions and directions in the running map
Write small spatial checks from the target relation
Score how well the updated map satisfies those checks
Reward moves that improve score and reduce contradictions because those moves strengthen the shared scene map
Learned exploration policy and final spatial answer

math.h2: The equation for dense spatial reward
math.words: Total reward combines final task success with the summed scores of intermediate spatial checks, so the agent is paid for map-improving moves before the episode ends.
symbols: reward for getting the final spatial question right
how strongly the learner values intermediate spatial checks
score at step t for how many checked spatial claims agree with the current map
the signal used to train the exploration policy

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Step 1: the agent turns left, sees only part of the scene, and 1 checked claim holds. Intermediate score: 1.
Step 2: the agent moves closer, reveals the hidden object, and 3 checked claims hold. Intermediate score: 3.
Step 3: the agent turns again and introduces a contradictory pose estimate, so only 2 claims hold. Intermediate score: 2.
If the final answer is correct, final reward is 10 and the three check scores sum to 6.
With check weight 2, total reward is 10 + 2 * 6 = 22.
A path with the same final answer but weaker intermediate checks gets less reward, so training prefers moves that build a cleaner map.

math.note: Dense checks speed learning because the agent can tell which earlier move improved spatial understanding instead of waiting until the end.

charts.title: Passive observer setup
charts.note: Without persistent mapping and dense checks, the agent forgets earlier evidence and struggles most when viewpoint matters.

charts.title: Active map-and-check setup
charts.note: The biggest gains appear on cases where moving to collect evidence and checking intermediate relations both matter.

items.html: If the vision system misreads object location or facing direction, the running map starts from the wrong state, so later checks reinforce a bad picture instead of a good one.
If the executable checks are too shallow, the agent can game them without truly improving the scene map, because it only needs to satisfy easy local conditions.
If the agent is allowed too few moves, it may never reach the views that resolve occlusion, so the map stays uncertain even with a good learning signal.
The method works best when object grounding is stable, the checked relations match the target task, and the agent is allowed enough movement to gather the missing evidence.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small grid-world room with a few objects, object directions, and partial views. Ask questions such as 'after turning right, is the lamp behind the chair?' Let the agent choose camera moves, keep a running object map, and score small relation checks after each move.

Compare three setups: final-answer reward only, running map without checked relations, and running map plus checked relations. The last setup should learn faster because each useful view earns credit before the episode ends, and it should answer more spatial questions correctly because the shared map preserves evidence across moves.
demo.metric_eq: answer_accuracy = correct_answers / total_questions and map_consistency_rate = verified_relation_checks / total_relation_checks
demo.closing: The demo should show that active exploration helps only when the agent can store what it found and score whether the new evidence made the spatial picture more coherent, because movement without memory and checks does not accumulate usable spatial evidence.
